chapter_theme: After the prince's death Chithirapathi begs the queen to release Manimekalai, warning through the old story of Killi and the Naga princess that the city's fate hangs on Indra's festival and on the goddess whose name the girl bears; the queen refuses the courtesan house, Aravanar comes and, answering the queen's wish for his long life, teaches that ageing and death are nature and sets out the twelve links and the ten evil deeds; Manimekalai takes leave and flies to Nagapuram, where Aputhiran is reborn as a king under whom rain never fails.

cast.role: Madhavi's mother, the old courtesan of Puhar who had plotted with the prince to get Manimekalai
the Chola queen, Udayakumaran's mother, who had imprisoned Manimekalai and now keeps her
a Chola king of Puhar of the past, in Chithirapathi's story, who loved the Naga princess in the seaside grove
the Naga princess, daughter of Valaivanan and Vasamayilai, who came to Killi and vanished
a sky-walking sage who tells Killi of Pilivalai and warns of the city's sinking
the dancer of Puhar, Manimekalai's mother, now a Buddhist renunciant
the aged Buddhist teacher of Puhar
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, a Buddhist renunciant who knows her former birth
an ascetic living in the flower grove outside Nagapuram

manimekalai:24:1-26.unit_note: End moved from 19 to 26: the sentence of line 19 (பொன்றினன் என்று) runs on into 20-22, and Chithirapathi's complaint closes at இடுக்கணும் உண்டால் (26), before the Killi story begins at 27.
manimekalai:24:1-26.reading: Shaken to hear that the prince, drawn by her scheme, has died by the vidyadhara's sword, the old courtesan falls at the queen's feet to get Madhavi's daughter out of prison, and laments that of all the hundred and twenty-one heavenly dancers cursed down to earth since the city arose, her line included, none suffered as she has: when the man who paid the flower-price died, Madhavi went into the monks' abode and the stage dancer took a bowl from house to house, a thing people only laugh at in courtesans; and besides the prince, she warns, the city faces a calamity through a woman.
manimekalai:24:1-26.nuance: The count adds up: eleven given to Indra, five born on earth for a slip in gesture, a hundred and four cursed with Indra's son, and Urvasi of her own line make the ஒன்று கடை நின்ற ஆறு இருபதின்மர் (6 x 20 + 1) of line 15. Chithirapathi measures disgrace by the courtesan line's own heavenly charter, not by any law of conduct; and her own scheme set the prince on the road to his death (lines 1-3), which she does not mention to the queen. Whose woman threatens the city (மாதரால், 25) is left open here; the story that follows is of Pilivalai, but lines 72-73 point at Manimekalai. The claim is answered by the queen at 77-82, who calls the courtesan's life itself base.
manimekalai:24:1-26.event: Hearing of the prince's death, Chithirapathi falls at the queen's feet to have Manimekalai released and laments Madhavi's turn to the begging bowl.

claims.claim: taking the begging bowl is unfitting for a dancing courtesan and earns only ridicule

manimekalai:24:27-51.unit_note: Moved: starts at 27, where the Killi story opens after Chithirapathi's warning, and ends at 51, where the king's question to the sage closes with அவன் உரைப்பான்; the core break at 44 fell mid-sentence (என்றே).
manimekalai:24:27-51.reading: Chithirapathi tells how the Chola Nedumudi Killi, in a lonely flowering grove of the seaside punnai shore in early spring, met a girl alone, was overcome by love through all five senses under Kama's flower-arrows, served her for a month without learning who she was, and, when she vanished, searched for her until a sky-walking sage appeared and the king bowed and asked him if he had seen her.
manimekalai:24:27-51.nuance: The king who 'saw the backs of many' and 'slew kings' (41, 45) is made to bow and serve; the five senses of 35-37 (seen, heard, eaten, breathed, touched) are the same five gates the Buddhist sermon of 101-122 will count among the links of birth, though Chithirapathi tells it as a love story.
manimekalai:24:27-51.event: In Chithirapathi's story, King Killi loves an unknown girl in a seaside grove for a month, loses her, and asks a sky-walking sage where she is.

manimekalai:24:52-74.unit_note: Moved: starts at 52 with the sage's answer and ends at 74, where Chithirapathi's whole speech closes with அஞ்சினேன் அரசன் தேவி! என்று ஏத்தி; the core break at 69 split the sage's warning from her fear that follows from it.
manimekalai:24:52-74.reading: Chithirapathi gives the sage's answer: the girl is Pilivalai, daughter of the Naga king Valaivanan, of whom it was foretold at her birth that she would unite with one of the sun's line and return with child, so she will not come back except with that son; and on the day the island's peace rite is not kept, Puhar will enter the sea, which the Manimekala goddess's word cannot stop because Indra's curse stands, so the king must never forget Vasava's festival; since then, she says, the city has never been free of dread, and she fears the great goddess may come if the girl who bears her name is harmed.
manimekalai:24:52-74.nuance: Chithirapathi's real argument is the last two lines: Manimekalai was named after the goddess, so harming her may bring the goddess, and the city's sinking is the threat behind her plea. The sage's warning is conditional, a rite to keep, unlike the fixed date given by the Buddhist sage of kaathai 9. Line 66 (ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்) is hard to place: 'that city' and 'this city' may be the Naga city and Puhar, or two moments of Puhar.
manimekalai:24:52-74.event: In Chithirapathi's story the sage names Pilivalai, foretells her son's coming, and warns that Puhar will sink into the sea if Indra's festival is ever neglected; Chithirapathi says she fears the goddess's coming.

claims.claim: the Manimekala goddess's word cannot undo Indra's curse on the city

manimekalai:24:75-88.unit_note: Moved: starts at 75 with Chithirapathi's request, after her speech closes at 74, and ends at 88 (தன்பால் வர), with Madhavi and Aravanar arriving before the queen; the core break at 89 split the list of those present (தேவியும் ஆயமும் சித்திராபதியும் / மாதவி மகளும்).
manimekalai:24:75-88.reading: Chithirapathi asks for the dancer whose mind has turned good to be given to her house, and the queen refuses: the girl fled the life of drink, lying, lust, killing and deceit that the wise renounce and that Chithirapathi's house takes as its chief, fearing it base, and she will stay with the queen; Madhavi, hearing of her daughter, troubled like a stirred pool and shaking like a wind-tossed branch, tells Sudhamathi, falls at Aravanar's feet and comes with him to the queen.
manimekalai:24:75-88.nuance: The queen, who had imprisoned Manimekalai, now speaks the renouncer's list against the courtesan's house; the five she names (கள், பொய், காமம், கொலை, உள்ளக் களவு) are close to the Buddhist precepts, but the unit attributes them only to உரவோர், 'the strong', so the claim is tagged general. நல் மனம் பிறந்த (75) is Chithirapathi's own phrase, used to win the girl back.
manimekalai:24:75-88.event: The queen refuses to hand Manimekalai to Chithirapathi; Madhavi, alarmed, brings Aravanar to the queen.

claims.claim: drink, lying, lust, killing and deceit are what the wise renounce, and a life built on them is base

manimekalai:24:89-100.unit_note: Start moved from 90 to 89 so that the list of those who rise (தேவியும் ஆயமும் சித்திராபதியும் / மாதவி மகளும்) is not split; the end at 100 is the core's.
manimekalai:24:89-100.reading: Seeing the sage, the queen, her women, Chithirapathi and Manimekalai rise and go to meet him and bow at his feet; he blesses them with 'may wisdom arise', and the queen seats him, washes his feet, honours him, and says her good deeds have brought him after many years and wishes his tired, aged body long life, though his tongue has not failed.
manimekalai:24:89-100.nuance: Even Chithirapathi rises and bows. The sage's blessing is for wisdom, the queen's for the body's long life; the next unit answers her wish.
manimekalai:24:89-100.event: All rise and bow to Aravanar, who blesses them; the queen washes his feet and wishes him long life.

claims.claim: a meeting with a holy man is the fruit of one's own good deeds

manimekalai:24:101-122.unit_note: End moved from 118 to 122: the six kinds of beings (115-118) are the subject of the sentence that runs to காட்டும் at 122, where they are born of good and bad deeds and taste joy and sorrow.
manimekalai:24:101-122.reading: Aravanar answers that though he lives in a body given to austerity he is like the setting sun, for to be born, grow old, fall ill and die is the nature of things, and he teaches the twelve links from ignorance through action, consciousness, name and form, the six gates, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming and birth to the fruit of deeds, saying that those who know them gain the great reward and those who don't go down to hell; ignorance is failing to know these, forgetting what is seen in the nature of things and trusting hearsay that a hare has horns; and living beings are of six kinds, born by good and bad deeds and shown joy and sorrow when the deeds ripen.
manimekalai:24:101-122.nuance: The queen's wish for long life is turned without rebuke into the first lesson: ageing is nature (இயல்பே, 104), not a misfortune to be wished away. The list of twelve ends with வினைப் பயன் where the old age and death of the usual list would be, and those come back as the opening sentence. Ignorance is defined epistemically, as trusting what one heard over what one saw (113-114), which kaathai 29's means of knowledge will develop.
manimekalai:24:101-122.event: Aravanar answers the queen's blessing and begins to teach the twelve links of dependent arising and the six kinds of beings.

claims.claim: whatever is born grows old, falls ill and dies by nature
birth runs through twelve linked conditions from ignorance to the fruit of deeds
those who know the twelve links gain the great reward and those who do not go to deep hell
ignorance is trusting hearsay over what is seen, like believing a hare has horns
beings are of six kinds, born by good and bad deeds, which ripen as joy and sorrow

manimekalai:24:123-140.unit_note: Moved: starts at 123 with the question on evil deeds, after the account of births closes at 122, and ends at 140, where the fruit of good deeds is eaten; the core break at 141 put the address to the queen (அரைசன் தேவியொடு ஆய் இழை நல்லீர்!) in this unit, apart from the கேண்மின் at 142 it belongs to.
manimekalai:24:123-140.reading: Aravanar defines evil deeds as ten: killing, theft and lustful desire of the body; lying, slander, harsh speech and idle speech of the tongue; and covetousness, anger and wrong view of the mind; the wise do not walk this way, and those who do are born as animals, ghosts and beings of hell in a troubled mind; good deeds are leaving these ten, keeping the precepts and standing first in giving, and those who do them are born as gods, humans and Brahmas and enjoy the fruit.
manimekalai:24:123-140.nuance: Good deeds here win only the higher births of the six, gods, humans and Brahmas; they do not end birth, which the previous unit ties to knowing the twelve links. The ten are counted by the door they come through (body, speech, mind), so wrong view (பொல்லாக் காட்சி) is itself a deed.

claims.claim: evil deeds are ten: three of the body, four of speech and three of the mind
those who do the ten are reborn as animals, ghosts and beings of hell
those who avoid the ten, keep the precepts and give are reborn as gods, humans and Brahmas and enjoy the fruit

manimekalai:24:141-158.unit_note: Moved: starts at 141 with Aravanar's address to the queen and her women, and ends at 158, where Manimekalai's farewell closes with அவரையும் வணங்கி; the core unit 142-161 cut the address from its verb and ran into the list of shrines (161-162).
manimekalai:24:141-158.reading: Aravanar bids the queen and the women hold to this dharma, and tells Manimekalai, who knows her former birth, that after she has heard the other doctrines he will tell her all of it in full; he rises, and she bows at his feet and tells the queen, the women and Chithirapathi not to forget his words, saying that if she stays they will call her death to the king's son, so she will go to Aputhiran's land, then worship at Manipallavam, then enter Vanji and do good deeds everywhere for the great pathini, and they need not grieve for her.
manimekalai:24:141-158.nuance: Aravanar's order is a method: Manimekalai is to hear the rival doctrines first and be taught the full dharma after (144), which is the shape of kaathais 27 to 30. Her own itinerary (153-156) names the next stages of the epic, and the pathini of Vanji is Kannaki, her father's wife.
manimekalai:24:141-158.event: Aravanar promises to teach Manimekalai fully later; she bows, takes leave of the queen and Chithirapathi, and says she will go to Aputhiran's land, Manipallavam and Vanji.

manimekalai:24:159-176.unit_note: Start moved from 162 to 159 so that the list of shrines she circles (உலக அறவியும் முதியாள் குடிகையும் / இலகு ஒளிக் கந்தமும்) is not split; the end at 176 is the kaathai's.
manimekalai:24:159-176.reading: At dusk Manimekalai circles and praises the world's charity hall, the old woman's shrine and the shining pillar, flies through the sky and comes down in a flower grove outside the great city of Indra's descendant, bows to an ascetic there and asks the city's name and king, and he tells her it is Nagapuram, ruled by Punniyarajan, son of Bhumichandran, since whose birth rain has never failed, earth and trees have yielded plenty and no wasting disease has touched living beings.
manimekalai:24:159-176.nuance: Punniyarajan is the reborn Aputhiran (the land she named at 153), and the city is called that of Indra's descendant (164): the plenty Indra once sent to idle Aputhiran's bowl now marks his birth as a king. The ascetic credits the rain to the king's birth, not to his rule.
manimekalai:24:159-176.event: Manimekalai flies from Puhar to a grove outside Nagapuram, where an ascetic tells her the city is ruled by Punniyarajan.

claims.claim: since a meritorious king's birth the rain has not failed and no disease has struck his people

links.note: The Silappathikaram gives Madhavi's descent from the maiden cursed to earth when Urvasi's dance failed before Indra as the pedigree of her art; Chithirapathi counts the same heavenly dancers, Urvasi of her own line, to measure her shame now that Madhavi begs.
links.teaches: The curse-myth that certifies the courtesan's art in the first epic becomes, in the second, the yardstick by which the courtesan house judges a daughter's renunciation as the worst fall of the line.

links.note: In the Silappathikaram, when Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma, the king and city grieve as men who have dropped a gem in the sea and the ascetics speak kind words; Chithirapathi says such a turn earns a courtesan only laughter.
links.teaches: Held together they show that the courtesan's renunciation has two publics: the city mourns the loss of beauty while the courtesan house reads the same act as ridicule, so neither epic's report of the town's reaction can be taken alone.

links.note: Both are a sage's warning that a city will sink: Brahmadharma gives Attipathi a fixed day and the king leads his people out, while the charana makes Puhar's sinking hang on a rite that must never be forgotten and that the goddess cannot override.
links.teaches: The pair shows the epic's two kinds of prophecy of ruin: a Buddhist sage's fixed fact that is escaped by leaving, and a curse tied to Indra's festival that is escaped only by unbroken observance, which is why the city's fate turns on the king's memory.

links.note: Kural 920 groups double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of men Fortune has left; the queen turns the charge on the courtesan house itself, a life built on drink, lies, lust and deceit, and from which a courtesan's own daughter flees in fear.
links.teaches: The couplet sees the courtesan only as a danger to the man, while the epic shows the same house as a danger to the women born in it, so that renunciation is a courtesan's escape, not only a patron's.

gains.a: a short traditional judgment that frames the queen's list as the old ethical verdict on the courtesan's world
gains.b: a case from inside the courtesan's house, where the harm falls on its daughter, which the couplet's man-centred warning never considers

links.note: Kural 351 says a base birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal as real; Aravanar puts ignorance first in the chain of birth and defines it as trusting hearsay that a hare has horns.
links.teaches: The couplet names unreal things taken as real without saying which; the epic gives the error a mechanism, hearsay preferred to what is seen, and a place, the first of twelve links, so the couplet's one step to birth becomes a chain.

gains.a: an older Tamil statement that ignorance is the root of birth, which shows the Buddhist chain speaking in a known idiom
gains.b: a definition of its மருள் by a stock example of an unreal thing (the hare's horn) and a causal sequence from error to birth

links.note: Tirumular nurtures the body because its perishing ends the life before true knowledge is won; when the queen wishes Aravanar's aged body long life, he answers that ageing and death are the nature of the born and turns to teaching.
links.teaches: The pair sets the Saiva siddha's body kept alive for knowledge against the Buddhist teacher's body let go because knowledge has been reached and must be passed on, so the worth of a long life depends on whether knowledge is still to be won.

gains.a: a contrary view that makes Aravanar's refusal of the blessing a position, not just an old man's modesty
gains.b: a teacher who has the knowledge and still declines the body's prolonging, which tests whether nurturing the body is a means or an end

links.note: Tirumular says those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet and its bliss; Aravanar counts the same sins among ten and says that leaving them, with precept and giving, wins only birth as god, human or Brahma.
links.teaches: The same abstentions are release in the Saiva verse and only a better birth in the Buddhist sermon, which places release in knowing the twelve links rather than in conduct; the pair shows that the two schools agree on the list and disagree on what it buys.

gains.a: a rival claim that abstaining from the great sins reaches the highest, which sharpens the epic's limit on what good deeds can do
gains.b: a finer count of the sins by body, speech and mind and a denial that abstention alone ends birth, against which its promise can be weighed

links.note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai that after she has heard the other doctrines he will teach her fully; in kaathai 27 she goes among the schools in Vanji and asks the Vedic logician his doctrine.
links.teaches: The survey of schools in kaathai 27 is set up here as a stage of instruction the teacher prescribes, so the rival doctrines are heard as preparation for the Buddhist teaching, not as free inquiry.

links.note: At Kannaki's shrine in Vanji the maid asks the pathini whether she has heard of Madhavi's and Manimekalai's renunciation; Manimekalai here resolves to go to Vanji and do good deeds for the great pathini.
links.teaches: The two epics meet at the Vanji shrine from both sides: the Silappathikaram brings news of the girl's renunciation to the pathini, and the Manimekalai sends the renounced girl to make merit for her.

links.note: Indra, to idle Aputhiran's bowl, sent rain until the land had no hungry; Aputhiran, reborn as Punniyarajan in the city of Indra's descendant, is a king since whose birth the rain has not failed.
links.teaches: The plenty that once mocked Aputhiran's charity by leaving no one to feed is now the sign of his merit as king, so the epic turns Indra's rival gift into the reward of the charity it tried to make useless.

links.note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre; the ascetic credits Nagapuram's unfailing rain to Punniyarajan's birth, before any rule.
links.teaches: Where the couplet makes a land's rain the fruit of a king's just rule, the epic makes it the fruit of his former birth's charity, moving the cause of plenty from the sceptre to karma.

gains.a: the rule against which the ascetic's claim stands out as a claim about birth, not governance
gains.b: a case where the king's plenty precedes any act of rule, showing a second source of the link between king and rain that the couplet does not name

new_concepts.gloss: dependent arising: the twelve linked conditions from ignorance to the fruit of deeds through which birth arises
new_concepts.label_source: label mine, the Manimekalai's term in kaathai 30; this unit lists the twelve (105-108) without the word

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: இந்திர சாபம் (65)

new_concepts.gloss: the festival; a public feast of a god or a town
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: வாசவன் விழாக் கோள் (69)

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: மா பத்தினி (155)

source_issues: Line 176 (அகை மலர்ப் பூம்பொழில் அருந் தவன் தான் என்) ends on என், a sentence that runs on into kaathai 25.
Line 66 (ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்) is hard to construe: which two cities are meant is not clear from the unit.
Lines 85 and 114 carry the repaired ௌ/ெள font flag (தெளியா, தெளிதல); the repaired readings make sense.
